statement: On a given straight line to describe a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.
heath_proof: Let AB be the given straight line, and the angle at C the given rectilineal angle; thus it is required to describe on the given straight line AB a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to the angle at C. The angle at C is then acute, or right, or obtuse. First let it be acute, and, as in the first figure, on the straight line AB, and at the point A, let the angle BAD be constructed equal to the angle at C; therefore the angle BAD is also acute. Let AE be drawn at right angles to DA, let AB be bisected at F, let FG be drawn from the point F at right angles to AB, and let GB be joined. Then, since AF is equal to FB, and FG is common, the two sides AF, FG are equal to the two sides BF, FG; and the angle AFG is equal to the angle BFG; therefore the base AG is equal to the base BG. [I. 4]  Therefore the circle described with centre G and distance GA will pass through B also. Let it be drawn, and let it be ABE; let EB be joined. Now, since AD is drawn from A, the extremity of the diameter AE, at right angles to AE, therefore AD touches the circle ABE. [III. 16]  Since then a straight line AD touches the circle ABE, and from the point of contact at A a straight line AB is drawn across in the circle ABE, the angle DAB is equal to the angle AEB in the alternate segment of the circle. [III. 32]  But the angle DAB is equal to the angle at C; therefore the angle at C is also equal to the angle AEB. Therefore on the given straight line AB the segment AEB of a circle has been described admitting the angle AEB equal to the given angle, the angle at C. Next let the angle at C be right; and let it be again required to describe on AB a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to the right angle at C. Let the angle BAD be constructed equal to the right angle at C, as is the case in the second figure; let AB be bisected at F, and with centre F and distance either FA or FB let the circle AEB be described. Therefore the straight line AD touches the circle ABE, because the angle at A is right. [III. 16] And the angle BAD is equal to the angle in the segment AEB, for the latter too is itself a right angle, being an angle in a semicircle. [III. 31] But the angle BAD is also equal to the angle at C. Therefore the angle AEB is also equal to the angle at C. Therefore again the segment AEB of a circle has been described on AB admitting an angle equal to the angle at C. Next, let the angle at C be obtuse; and on the straight line AB, and at the point A, let the angle BAD be constructed equal to it, as is the case in the third figure; let AE be drawn at right angles to AD, let AB be again bisected at F, let FG be drawn at right angles to AB, and let GB be joined. Then, since AF is again equal to FB, and FG is common, the two sides AF, FG are equal to the two sides BF, FG; and the angle AFG is equal to the angle BFG; therefore the base AG is equal to the base BG. [I. 4]  Therefore the circle described with centre G and distance GA will pass through B also; let it so pass, as AEB. Now, since AD is drawn at right angles to the diameter AE from its extremity, AD touches the circle AEB. [III. 16]  And AB has been drawn across from the point of contact at A; therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle constructed in the alternate segment AHB of the circle. [III. 32]  But the angle BAD is equal to the angle at C. Therefore the angle in the segment AHB is also equal to the angle at C. Therefore on the given straight line AB the segment AHB of a circle has been described admitting an angle equal to the angle at C.
ai_proof_text:
3.33
**Statement:** On a given straight line to describe a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

Let AB be the given straight line and C the given rectilineal angle. It is required to describe on AB a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to C. The angle C is either acute, right, or obtuse; the three cases are treated in turn.

**Case I: the angle C is acute.**

**Step 1.** On the straight line AB and at the point A on it, construct the angle BAD equal to the angle C [1.23].

**Step 2.** From the point A draw AK at right angles to AD [1.11], taking AK on the same side of AD as B. Since the angle BAD (being equal to the acute angle C) is less than the right angle DAK, and AB, AK lie on the same side of AD, the straight line AB falls within the angle DAK; hence the angle BAK is the excess of the right angle DAK over the angle BAD, and so the angle BAK is less than a right angle.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at the point F [1.10], and from F draw FG at right angles to AB [1.11], taking FG on the same side of AB as K.

**Step 4.** The straight line AB falls on the two straight lines AK and FG and makes with them the interior angles BAK and AFG on the same side; the angle BAK is less than a right angle (Step 2) and the angle AFG is right (Step 3), so together they are less than two right angles. Therefore AK and FG, being produced, meet on that side [P5]; let them meet at the point G. Join GB [P1].

**Step 5.** Since AF is equal to FB (Step 3) and FG is common, the two sides AF, FG are equal to the two sides BF, FG respectively; and the angle AFG is equal to the angle BFG, both being right angles [P4]. Therefore the base AG is equal to the base BG [1.4].

**Step 6.** With centre G and distance GA describe a circle [P3]. Since GB is equal to GA (Step 5), the point B lies on the circumference of this circle [D1.15]. Produce AG beyond G [P2] until it meets the circumference again at the point E; then AE, passing through the centre G and terminated in both directions by the circumference, is a diameter of the circle [D1.17]. The figure contained by the straight line AB and the circumference AEB is a segment of the circle on AB [D3.6].

**Step 7.** The straight line AD was drawn from A at right angles to AK (Step 2), and the diameter AE lies along AK; thus AD is drawn from the extremity A of the diameter AE at right angles to that diameter. Therefore AD touches the circle at A [3.16, Porism].

**Step 8.** Since AB falls within the angle DAK (Step 2), the ray AK, and hence the point E on it, lies on the opposite side of AB from D; so the segment AEB is the segment alternate to the angle DAB. Now AD touches the circle at A, and from the point of contact A the straight line AB has been drawn across in the circle, cutting it; therefore the angle DAB, which AB makes with the tangent AD, is equal to the angle in the alternate segment AEB, that is, to the angle AEB [3.32], which is the angle in the segment AEB [D3.8].

**Step 9.** But the angle DAB is equal to the angle C (Step 1); therefore the angle AEB is also equal to the angle C [CN1]. Hence on the given straight line AB the segment AEB of a circle has been described admitting the angle AEB equal to the given angle C.

**Case II: the angle C is right.**

**Step 10.** Bisect AB at the point F [1.10], and with centre F and distance FA describe a circle [P3]. Since FB is equal to FA, the point B lies on the circumference [D1.15]. Thus AB passes through the centre F and is terminated in both directions by the circumference, so AB is a diameter [D1.17], and the figure contained by AB and the circumference cut off by it on either side is a semicircle [D1.18]; let E be any point on this circumference, and join AE, EB [P1].

**Step 11.** The angle AEB, being the angle in the semicircle AEB, is a right angle [3.31]. But the angle C is also a right angle, and all right angles are equal to one another [P4]; therefore the angle AEB is equal to the angle C. Hence on AB the semicircle AEB has been described admitting the angle AEB equal to the given angle C.

**Case III: the angle C is obtuse.**

**Step 12.** On AB at the point A construct the angle BAD equal to the angle C [1.23], and from A draw AK at right angles to AD [1.11], taking AK on the same side of AD as B. Since the right angle DAK is less than the obtuse angle DAB, and AK, AB lie on the same side of AD, the straight line AK falls within the angle DAB; hence the angle KAB is the excess of the angle DAB over the right angle DAK. Since the angle DAB, being a rectilineal angle, is less than two right angles, the angle KAB is less than a right angle.

**Step 13.** Bisect AB at F [1.10], and from F draw FG at right angles to AB [1.11] on the same side of AB as K. The straight line AB falls on AK and FG and makes the interior angles KAB (less than a right angle) and AFG (right) on the same side, together less than two right angles; therefore AK and FG, being produced, meet on that side [P5]; let them meet at G. Join GB [P1].

**Step 14.** As in Step 5, AF is equal to FB, FG is common, and the right angles AFG, BFG are equal [P4]; therefore AG is equal to BG [1.4]. With centre G and distance GA describe a circle [P3]; since GB is equal to GA, B lies on its circumference [D1.15]. Produce AG beyond G [P2] to meet the circumference at E; then AE is a diameter [D1.17], lying along AK, and AD is drawn from its extremity A at right angles to it; therefore AD touches the circle at A [3.16, Porism].

**Step 15.** In this case AK falls within the angle DAB (Step 12), so K, and with it G and E, lie on the same side of AB as D; the segment alternate to the angle DAB is therefore the segment on the other side of AB. Let H be any point on the circumference on that other side of AB, and join AH, HB [P1]; then AHB is a segment of the circle on AB [D3.6] and the angle AHB is the angle in it [D3.8]. Since AD touches the circle at A and AB is drawn across in the circle from the point of contact, the angle DAB is equal to the angle AHB in the alternate segment AHB [3.32].

**Step 16.** But the angle DAB is equal to the angle C (Step 12); therefore the angle AHB is equal to the angle C [CN1]. Hence on AB the segment AHB of a circle has been described admitting the angle AHB equal to the given angle C.

**Step 17.** Therefore in every case, on the given straight line AB a segment of a circle has been described admitting an angle equal to the given rectilineal angle C. Q.E.F.

*Path note:* in Case II the most direct route is taken: the semicircle on AB is described at once and its angle is shown right by 3.31, so neither the construction of the angle BAD nor the tangent AD is needed there; the tangent-and-alternate-segment argument (3.16 Por., 3.32) is used only in the acute and obtuse cases, where it is indispensable.
